summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change turns a strict origin allowlist into reflect-any-origin CORS while keeping credentialed access enabled.

## Why this is blocking

`corsHeaders` previously only emitted `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` when `origin` was in `ALLOWED` (`https://app.example.com`). The new code always returns:

- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <request Origin or *>`
- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`

In a browser, that means any hostile page can issue credentialed cross-origin requests (cookies / `Authorization` in credentialed mode) and **read the response**. That is a full break of the same-origin boundary the old allowlist enforced.

The mobile rationale does not justify this:

- Native HTTP clients are not subject to CORS; they never needed `Access-Control-*` headers.
- Mobile **webviews** that do use the browser CORS model still need an explicit allowlist (app origin, custom scheme, or known hosts), not a universal reflect.

Secondary issue on the same path: when `origin` is null, the function emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, which is invalid per the Fetch CORS rules and will be rejected by browsers — so the null-origin branch neither helps mobile nor stays spec-correct.

## Recommendation

Restore an explicit allowlist (extend it with real mobile-webview origins if needed). Keep credentials only for listed origins. Do not reflect arbitrary `Origin` values.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: The change removed the origin allowlist and now always sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the request Origin (or *) together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, enabling credentialed cross-origin reads from any site. Base code only reflected allowlisted origins.
